claims.claim: Flamenco (flam) is the principal source of piRNAs in the somatic follicle cells that enclose egg chambers.
claims.source: Of the two Drosophila uni-strand clusters, flamenco (flam) is the principal source of piRNAs in the somatic follicle cells that enclose egg chambers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009) and was originally identified as a master regulator of gypsy retrotransposons (Mével-Ninio et al., 2007; Pélisson et al., 1994; Prud'homme et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Flamenco was originally identified as a master regulator of gypsy retrotransposons.
claims.source: Of the two Drosophila uni-strand clusters, flamenco (flam) is the principal source of piRNAs in the somatic follicle cells that enclose egg chambers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009) and was originally identified as a master regulator of gypsy retrotransposons (Mével-Ninio et al., 2007; Pélisson et al., 1994; Prud'homme et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Flamenco covers up to ~650 kb of pericentromeric heterochromatin of chromosome X.
claims.source: Being an unusually large transcriptional unit, flam covers up to ~650 kb of pericentromeric heterochromatin of chromosome X and depends on conventional RNA export mechanisms, centred on the nuclear export factor heterodimer Nxf1/Nxt1 (Dennis et al., 2016; Herold et al., 2001; Tutucci and Stutz, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Flamenco depends on conventional RNA export mechanisms, centred on the nuclear export factor heterodimer Nxf1/Nxt1.
claims.source: Being an unusually large transcriptional unit, flam covers up to ~650 kb of pericentromeric heterochromatin of chromosome X and depends on conventional RNA export mechanisms, centred on the nuclear export factor heterodimer Nxf1/Nxt1 (Dennis et al., 2016; Herold et al., 2001; Tutucci and Stutz, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Upon export, flam transcripts localise to perinuclear Yb-bodies, where they are thought to be licensed for piRNA biogenesis.
claims.source: Upon export, flam transcripts localise to perinuclear Yb-bodies, where they are thought to be licensed for piRNA biogenesis (Hirakata et al., 2019; Murano et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2011; Saito et al., 2010), though the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, though the mechanism is not fully understood.

claims.claim: Yb-bodies are cytoplasmic, perinuclear condensates of the DEAD-box RNA helicase Yb.
claims.source: Yb-bodies are cytoplasmic, perinuclear condensates of the DEAD-box RNA helicase Yb, encoded by the fs(1)Yb gene, which is exclusively expressed in somatic follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Hirakata et al., 2019; Olivieri et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2011; Saito et al., 2010; Szakmary et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Yb is encoded by the fs(1)Yb gene, which is exclusively expressed in somatic follicle cells.
claims.source: Yb-bodies are cytoplasmic, perinuclear condensates of the DEAD-box RNA helicase Yb, encoded by the fs(1)Yb gene, which is exclusively expressed in somatic follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Hirakata et al., 2019; Olivieri et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2011; Saito et al., 2010; Szakmary et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Yb is essential for somatic piRNA production.
claims.source: Yb is essential for somatic piRNA production, and its assembly into Yb-bodies does not depend on any known piRNA biogenesis factor, and therefore is at the apex of the piRNA biogenesis protein network (Hirakata et al., 2019; Ishizu et al., 2015; Ishizu et al., 2019; Murota et al., 2014; Olivieri et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Yb assembly into Yb-bodies does not depend on any known piRNA biogenesis factor.
claims.source: Yb is essential for somatic piRNA production, and its assembly into Yb-bodies does not depend on any known piRNA biogenesis factor, and therefore is at the apex of the piRNA biogenesis protein network (Hirakata et al., 2019; Ishizu et al., 2015; Ishizu et al., 2019; Murota et al., 2014; Olivieri et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Yb is at the apex of the piRNA biogenesis protein network.
claims.source: Yb is essential for somatic piRNA production, and its assembly into Yb-bodies does not depend on any known piRNA biogenesis factor, and therefore is at the apex of the piRNA biogenesis protein network (Hirakata et al., 2019; Ishizu et al., 2015; Ishizu et al., 2019; Murota et al., 2014; Olivieri et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Yb assembly is independent of other piRNA factors, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Yb-bodies possess biophysical properties typical of phase-separated condensates.
claims.source: Yb-bodies have been reported to possess biophysical properties typical of phase-separated condensates, which likely facilitate the biochemical processes happening in these foci (Hirakata et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The formation of Yb-bodies depends on flam RNA.
claims.source: Given that flam is the major piRNA source locus in somatic follicle cells, we and others have found that the formation of Yb-bodies depends on flam RNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Dennis et al., 2016; Hirakata et al., 2019; Sokolova et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work, supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: flamBG carries a P-element insertion in the putative promoter of flamenco.
claims.source: Two previously described flam mutant alleles (Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009; Mével-Ninio et al., 2007) disrupt piRNA cluster transcription via P-element insertions near the 5′ end: flamBG, carrying an insertion in the putative promoter, and flamKG, carrying an insertion immediately downstream of the TSS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the flamBG allele, supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: flamKG carries a P-element insertion immediately downstream of the TSS of flamenco.
claims.source: Two previously described flam mutant alleles (Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009; Mével-Ninio et al., 2007) disrupt piRNA cluster transcription via P-element insertions near the 5′ end: flamBG, carrying an insertion in the putative promoter, and flamKG, carrying an insertion immediately downstream of the TSS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the flamKG allele, supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Trans-heterozygous flamBG/KG flies show strong de-repression of somatic, gypsy-family TEs.
claims.source: These mutants show strong de-repression of somatic, gypsy-family TEs (Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009; Mével-Ninio et al., 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), which is accompanied by a disassembly of Yb-bodies, despite some of the protein still being present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Trans-heterozygous flamBG/KG flies show disassembly of Yb-bodies, despite some of the protein still being present.
claims.source: These mutants show strong de-repression of somatic, gypsy-family TEs (Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009; Mével-Ninio et al., 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), which is accompanied by a disassembly of Yb-bodies, despite some of the protein still being present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by figure references.

claims.claim: The production of piRNAs derived from the 3′ UTR of coding genes is unchanged in flamBG/KG mutants.
claims.source: Notably, the production of other classes of piRNAs, such as those derived from the 3′ UTR of coding genes, is unchanged in these mutants (Hirakata et al., 2019; Sokolova et al., 2019), further underscoring a link between flam and Yb-bodies.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Knockdowns of nxf1/nxt1 in OSCs compromise Yb-bodies formation.
claims.source: Knockdowns of nxf1/nxt1 in ovarian somatic cells (OSCs), a cell line derived from the somatic compartment of the ovary that expresses a functional piRNA pathway (Saito et al., 2009), also compromise Yb-bodies formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, H), with similar results reported in soma-specific knockdowns in ovaries (Dennis et al., 2016; Sokolova et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: The production and localisation of flam transcripts to Yb-bodies and the assembly of those structures are interdependent.
claims.source: These results, together with previous findings (Dennis et al., 2016; Hirakata et al., 2019; Sokolova et al., 2019), suggest that the production and localisation of flam transcripts to Yb-bodies and the assembly of those structures are interdependent.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Various Nups have been ascribed gene regulatory functions, often via chromatin binding.
claims.source: Various Nups have been ascribed gene regulatory functions, often via chromatin binding (Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010), and a subset of NPC subunits has been genetically implicated in transposon control in Drosophila ovaries (Czech et al., 2013; Handler et al., 2013; Muerdter et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: A subset of NPC subunits has been genetically implicated in transposon control in Drosophila ovaries.
claims.source: Various Nups have been ascribed gene regulatory functions, often via chromatin binding (Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010), and a subset of NPC subunits has been genetically implicated in transposon control in Drosophila ovaries (Czech et al., 2013; Handler et al., 2013; Muerdter et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Knockdown of most Nups resulted in pronounced cell death and disassembled Yb-bodies, with little to no effect on TEs.
claims.source: Knockdown of most Nups resulted in pronounced cell death and disassembled Yb-bodies, with little to no effect on TEs (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Loss of subunits of the Nup62 sub-complex (Nup54-Nup58-Nup62) and their scaffold Nup93-1 caused strong TE de-repression.
claims.source: Instead, loss of subunits of the Nup62 sub-complex (Nup54-Nup58-Nup62) and their scaffold Nup93-1 (Chug et al., 2015; Stuwe et al., 2015; Ulrich et al., 2014) caused strong TE de-repression (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Only the depletion of Nup54 and Nup58 resulted in TE up-regulation without severely affecting cell viability.
claims.source: Among these, only the depletion of Nup54 and Nup58 resulted in TE up-regulation without severely affecting cell viability (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), potentially hinting to an effect distinct from general nuclear transport.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Yb-bodies were dispersed in siNup54 and siNup58 cells.
claims.source: Yb-bodies were also dispersed in siNup54 and siNup58 and residual Yb was visible only at increased laser power, despite an overall minor effect on Yb protein levels (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: TE de-repression caused by knockdown of nup54 and nup58 was comparable to that observed upon depletion of Nxt1.
claims.source: Of note, TE de-repression caused by knockdown of nup54 and nup58 was comparable to that observed upon depletion of Nxt1 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), reported to also function in the co-transcriptional gene silencing branch of the piRNA pathway (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019; Murano et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Loss of TE silencing upon depletion of most Nups is likely a result of the general NPC function in gene expression.
claims.source: These data indicate that loss of TE silencing upon depletion of most Nups is likely a result of the general NPC function in gene expression, whereas Nup54 and Nup58 seem to have more specific roles in transposon control.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 seem to have more specific roles in transposon control.
claims.source: These data indicate that loss of TE silencing upon depletion of most Nups is likely a result of the general NPC function in gene expression, whereas Nup54 and Nup58 seem to have more specific roles in transposon control.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Cells depleted of Nup54 or Nup58 showed a strong increase in the expression of gypsy-family TEs.
claims.source: Cells depleted of Nup54 or Nup58 showed a strong increase in the expression of gypsy-family TEs, which are known to be expressed in the somatic compartment of the ovary and regulated by flam (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D; Lécher et al., 1997; Pélisson et al., 1994; Prud'homme et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: The spectrum of TEs affected and the magnitude of de-repression in siNup54 and siNup58 were very similar to those observed in yb knockdowns.
claims.source: Both the spectrum of TEs affected and the magnitude of de-repression were very similar to those observed in yb knockdowns.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: siNup54 and siNup58 had only a moderate impact on protein-coding genes, with 42 genes de-regulated in each.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed only a moderate impact on protein-coding genes, with 130 genes de-regulated in siYb (more than fourfold and adjusted p value < 0.05), 42 in siNup54, and 42 in siNup58 (Figure 1D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of genes up-regulated by more than fourfold in siNup54 and siNup58 is found nearby transposon insertions.
claims.source: A substantial fraction of those genes up-regulated by more than fourfold is found nearby transposon insertions that become de-silenced when the piRNA pathway is compromised (49/126 or 39% in siYb, 16/39 or 41% in siNup54, 13/40 or 33% in siNup58) (Figure 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Most of the gene expression changes observed upon siNup54 and siNup58 knockdowns are a consequence of TE re-activation.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that most of the gene expression changes observed upon these knockdowns are in fact a consequence of TE re-activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that many de-regulated genes are near TE insertions.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nup62 and nup93-1 caused more pronounced mis-expression of protein-coding genes than siNup54 and siNup58.
claims.source: Although knockdown of nup62 and nup93-1 also caused de-repression of some flam-regulated TEs, we found much more pronounced mis-expression of protein-coding genes, with 207 genes de-regulated in siNup62 and 417 in siNup93-1 (more than fourfold and adjusted p value < 0.05) (Figure 1G, H), which could not be explained by proximity to nearby TE insertions.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: siNup62 and siNup93-1 resulted in de-repression of TEs that are not normally subject to piRNA-mediated silencing in somatic cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, this was accompanied by de-repression of TEs that are not normally subject to piRNA-mediated silencing in somatic cells, for example, R2-element (Figure 1G, H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: siNup62 and siNup93-1 resulted in expression changes of other Nups, RNA export factors, and Yb.
claims.source: Of note, siNup62 and siNup93-1 resulted in expression changes of other Nups, RNA export factors, and Yb, presumably via indirect effects on nuclear transport and/or gene expression (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by a figure reference.

claims.claim: In somatic follicle cells, Nup54 and Nup58 play specialised roles dedicated to transposon silencing, distinct from Nup62 and Nup93-1.
claims.source: Considered together, our results indicate that, in somatic follicle cells, Nup54 and Nup58 play specialised roles dedicated to transposon silencing, distinct from Nup62 and Nup93-1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing different Nup knockdowns.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 belong to the highly conserved class of 'FG-Nups'.
claims.source: Nup54 and Nup58 belong to the highly conserved class of 'FG-Nups' (Beck and Hurt, 2017; Figure 2A) and constitute the heterotrimeric Nup62 complex (Nup54-Nup58-Nup62) (Chug et al., 2015; Stuwe et al., 2015; Ulrich et al., 2014) that lines the inner channel of the NPC (Beck and Hurt, 2017; Grandi et al., 1995; Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 constitute the heterotrimeric Nup62 complex (Nup54-Nup58-Nup62) that lines the inner channel of the NPC.
claims.source: Nup54 and Nup58 belong to the highly conserved class of 'FG-Nups' (Beck and Hurt, 2017; Figure 2A) and constitute the heterotrimeric Nup62 complex (Nup54-Nup58-Nup62) (Chug et al., 2015; Stuwe et al., 2015; Ulrich et al., 2014) that lines the inner channel of the NPC (Beck and Hurt, 2017; Grandi et al., 1995; Kim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and a figure reference.

claims.claim: The FG repeats of the Nup62 complex subunits contribute to the selective permeability barrier of the NPC and interact with nuclear transport receptors, such as Nxf1.
claims.source: The phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats of the Nup62 complex subunits contribute to the selective permeability barrier of the NPC and interact with nuclear transport receptors, such as Nxf1 (Köhler and Hurt, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: RNA-seq showed a reduction in steady-state levels of flam transcript upon nup54, nup58, nup62, nup93-1, and yb knockdowns in OSCs.
claims.source: Our RNA-seq showed a reduction in steady-state levels of flam transcript upon nup54, nup58, nup62, nup93-1, and yb knockdowns in OSCs (Figure 1D-H, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: The reduction in flam transcript levels was specific to flam as other somatic piRNA source loci were unaffected.
claims.source: This was both specific to flam as other somatic piRNA source loci (e.g. the protein-coding gene tj or the piRNA cluster 20A) were unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), and unexpected since prior studies had shown accumulation of flam transcripts in cases where its conversion into piRNAs was disrupted, for example, by knockdown of the ribonuclease zuc (Murota et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Depletion of Yb, Nup54, and Nup58 revealed a reduction in flam RNA that was more pronounced towards the 3′ end of flam.
claims.source: In contrast, depletion of Yb, Nup54, and Nup58 revealed a reduction that was more pronounced towards the 3′ end of flam (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: In nup62 and nup93-1 knockdowns, reduced flam RNA levels were uniform.
claims.source: In nup62 and nup93-1 knockdowns, reduced RNA levels were uniform, again highlighting a different role for these Nups (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nup54, nup58, or yb had little to no effect on PRO-seq signal around the transcription initiation site or within the first 10 kb and 40 kb of flam.
claims.source: Knockdown of nup54, nup58, or yb had little to no effect on either signal around the transcription initiation site or within the first 10 kb and 40 kb of flam, whereas a more pronounced decrease in siYb cells was observed upon inspection of the entire locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on PRO-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Global PRO-seq signal from protein-coding genes and cluster 20A was unchanged upon nup54, nup58, or yb knockdown.
claims.source: In contrast, global PRO-seq signal from protein-coding genes and cluster 20A was unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on PRO-seq data, supported by a figure reference.

claims.claim: Loss of Nup54 or Nup58 reduces the stability of flam transcripts, with larger effects on regions distal from the transcription initiation sites.
claims.source: Overall, these observations are consistent with a hypothesis that loss of Nup54 or Nup58 reduces the stability of flam transcripts, with larger effects on regions distal from the transcription initiation sites.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the RNA-seq and PRO-seq data.

claims.claim: Depletion of Yb caused a collapse in the antisense, TE-targeting piRNA population, but left 21-nt siRNAs unaffected.
claims.source: As previously reported (Hirakata et al., 2019), depletion of Yb caused a collapse in the antisense, TE-targeting piRNA population, but leaving 21-nt siRNAs unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study and previous work, supported by a citation and figure references.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nup54 and nup58 resulted in a approximately threefold decrease in antisense piRNAs, highly specific to those derived from flam.
claims.source: Knockdown of nup54 and nup58 resulted in a approximately threefold decrease in antisense piRNAs, but this impact was highly specific to those derived from flam (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on small RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: piRNAs derived from tj and cluster 20A were unaffected or slightly more abundant upon nup54 and nup58 knockdown.
claims.source: In contrast, piRNAs derived from tj and cluster 20A were unaffected or slightly more abundant (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on small RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: siYb had a general impact on piRNA production, in line with its role as key biogenesis factor.
claims.source: Whilst siYb had a general impact on piRNA production, in line with its role as key biogenesis factor (Hirakata et al., 2019; Ishizu et al., 2015; Ishizu et al., 2019; Murota et al., 2014; Olivieri et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2010), siNup54 and siNup58 only showed a reduction of flam-derived piRNAs (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on small RNA-seq data, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: piRNAs were lost homogenously along the entire flam cluster in siYb.
claims.source: Binning analysis of the flam locus showed that piRNAs were lost homogenously along the entire cluster in siYb (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), unlike the precursor transcript levels measured by RNA-seq, indicating that no processing can occur in the absence of Yb.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on small RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: piRNA loss upon nup54 and nup58 knockdown was more pronounced towards the 3′ region of flam.
claims.source: In contrast, piRNA loss upon nup54 and nup58 knockdown was more pronounced towards the 3′ region (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), mirroring the precursor transcript reduction observed by RNA-seq.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on small RNA-seq data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: Depletion of Nup54 and Nup58 resulted in clustering of flam RNA signal in one predominant focus within the nuclear envelope.
claims.source: Depletion of Nup54 and Nup58 resulted in clustering of the signal in one predominant focus within the nuclear envelope (Figure 2I–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-FISH data, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: The flam RNA nuclear focus likely corresponds to flam RNPs stalled prior to nuclear export.
claims.source: Since the flam DNA locus is located at the nuclear periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C), this RNA nuclear focus likely corresponds to flam RNPs stalled prior to nuclear export (Dennis et al., 2016; Dennis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-FISH data and the known location of the flam locus, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Neither nup54 nor nup58 knockdown affected the distribution of bulk polyadenylated mRNAs.
claims.source: Of note, neither nup54 nor nup58 knockdown affected the distribution of bulk polyadenylated mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), unlike depletion of Nxf1 or Nxt1, which instead resulted in nuclear retention of newly synthesised mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2M), as reported (Herold et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on RNA-FISH data, supported by citations and figure references.

claims.claim: Transposon silencing defects resulting from loss of Nup54 or Nup58 arise from their role in facilitating flam export from the nucleus.
claims.source: Considered together, these results indicate that transposon silencing defects resulting from loss of Nup54 or Nup58 arise from their role in facilitating flam export from the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 might be required to ensure processivity of nuclear export of the long flam transcript.
claims.source: Given that the effect is most prominent on the 3′ end of the transcript, we hypothesise that Nup54 and Nup58 might be required to ensure processivity of nuclear export of this, otherwise unstable, long transcript.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that the 3′ end of flam is most affected.

claims.claim: Residual flam molecules that reach the cytosol upon siNup54 and siNup58 might still be processed by Yb, although with lower efficiency than within properly formed Yb-bodies.
claims.source: In this scenario, residual flam molecules (likely corresponding to the 5′ portion of the cluster) that reach the cytosol upon siNup54 and siNup58 might still be processed by Yb, although with lower efficiency than within properly formed Yb-bodies.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that some piRNAs are still produced.

claims.claim: Deleting the FG-repeats in Nup54 and Nup58 (∆FG) had little effect on their TE silencing capability compared to FL Nups.
claims.source: Likewise, deleting the FG-repeats in Nup54 and Nup58 (∆FG) had little effect on their TE silencing capability compared to FL Nups.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 lacking the C-terminal domain (∆C) failed to rescue transposon de-repression.
claims.source: In contrast, Nup54 and Nup58 lacking the C-terminal domain (∆C) failed to rescue transposon de-repression (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on rescue experiments, supported by figure references.

claims.claim: The ability to interact with the other Nups is required to ensure TE silencing by Nup54 and Nup58.
claims.source: These results suggest that the ability to interact with the other Nups is required to ensure TE silencing, and thus that Nup54 and Nup58 carry out this function from within the NPC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that the C-terminal domain is required.

claims.claim: Nup54 and Nup58 carry out their TE silencing function from within the NPC.
claims.source: These results suggest that the ability to interact with the other Nups is required to ensure TE silencing, and thus that Nup54 and Nup58 carry out this function from within the NPC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: The nup54MB allele produces a truncated protein lacking the carboxy-terminal region due to a Mi{ET1} transposon insertion.
claims.source: One such exception, the nup54MB003363 (nup54MB) allele, produces a truncated protein lacking the carboxy-terminal region due to a Mi{ET1} transposon insertion (Nallasivan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the nup54MB allele, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The nup54MB truncated protein fails to co-precipitate with Nup58.
claims.source: This shortened Nup54 protein lacks the Nup54-family domain (Figure 3A, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and fails to co-precipitate with Nup58 (Figure 3E), as expected from earlier reports (Chug et al., 2015).

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 are specifically required for transposon silencing in Drosophila ovarian follicle cells. Knockdown of Nup54 and Nup58 resulted in TE up-regulation without severely affecting cell viability, dispersed Yb-bodies, and a strong increase in gypsy-family TE expression, with effects comparable to Yb knockdown but distinct from other Nup knockdowns (Nup62, Nup93-1) which caused widespread gene expression changes and cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C46-C61 collectively demonstrate that Nup54 and Nup58 have specialized roles in transposon control distinct from other NPC subunits. The RNA-seq data (C53-C60), cell viability assays (C46-C48), and Yb-body imaging (C49) provide converging evidence. The comparison with other Nup knockdowns strengthens the specificity claim.

results.result: Loss of Nup54 or Nup58 reduces flam transcript stability with a 3' bias. RNA-seq showed reduced steady-state flam levels specifically (other piRNA loci unaffected), with reduction more pronounced toward the 3' end. PRO-seq data showed minimal effects on transcription initiation, suggesting the reduction stems from transcript instability rather than decreased transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are supported by complementary RNA-seq and PRO-seq data showing flam-specific effects with 3' bias. The binning analysis (C67) and PRO-seq controls (C69-C70) strengthen the interpretation that this reflects post-transcriptional instability rather than transcriptional defects. The hypothesis in C71 is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 knockdown specifically reduces flam-derived piRNAs with a 3' bias. Small RNA-seq showed approximately threefold decrease in flam-derived antisense piRNAs, while piRNAs from other loci (tj, 20A) were unaffected. The piRNA loss was more pronounced toward the 3' region of flam, mirroring the precursor transcript reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are well-supported by small RNA-seq data with appropriate controls (other piRNA sources). The 3' bias in piRNA loss (C77) mirrors the transcript reduction pattern, providing internal consistency. The specificity to flam-derived piRNAs (C73-C74) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 facilitate flam export from the nucleus. RNA-FISH showed clustering of flam RNA in nuclear foci upon Nup54/58 depletion, likely representing stalled export, while bulk mRNA distribution was unaffected. This indicates transposon silencing defects arise from impaired flam-specific export rather than general nuclear transport defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by RNA-FISH data showing flam-specific nuclear retention (C78-C79) with appropriate controls showing normal bulk mRNA distribution (C80). The conclusion (C81) logically follows from the data. The inference about stalled export (C79) is reasonable given the known nuclear peripheral location of the flam locus.

results.result: The C-terminal domain of Nup54 and Nup58, but not the FG-repeats, is required for TE silencing function. Rescue experiments showed that deletion of FG-repeats had little effect on TE silencing capability, while C-terminal deletion failed to rescue. This suggests Nup54/58 function from within the NPC through interactions with other Nups rather than through FG-repeat-mediated transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87, C96-C97 are supported by systematic domain deletion and rescue experiments. The requirement for the C-terminal domain (C85-C86) and dispensability of FG-repeats (C84, C97) is clearly demonstrated. The inference that function occurs within the NPC (C87) is reasonable given the requirement for Nup-Nup interactions.

results.result: The nup54MB hypomorphic allele phenocopies Nup54 knockdown effects in vivo. Trans-heterozygous nup54MB/9B4 flies showed TE de-repression, reduced flam RNA levels (with 3' bias), reduced Yb-bodies, while dual-strand piRNA cluster expression was unchanged. The truncated Nup54MB protein lacks the C-terminal domain and fails to interact with Nup58.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C95 provide in vivo validation of the cell culture findings. The molecular characterization of the allele (C88-C89), phenotypic analysis (C90-C91, C94), and specificity to flam (C92) are well-documented. The inference about compromised flam export (C95) is consistent with the overall model.

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 physically interact with both Yb and Nxf1/Nxt1. PL-MS showed Yb was highly enriched in Nup54/58 pulldowns, along with NPC components and modest Nxf1 enrichment. Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed interactions with Yb, Nxf1, and Nxt1, with the Yb interaction being RNA-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107, C111-C114 are supported by complementary PL-MS and co-IP data. The RNA-independence of the Nup54/58-Yb interaction (C113-C114) is demonstrated by RNase treatment. The detection of both nuclear (Nxf1/Nxt1) and cytoplasmic (Yb) factors supports the bridging function proposed.

results.result: The HelC domain of Yb is partially responsible for anchoring Yb to the NPC. Deletion of the HelC domain weakened but did not abolish the Yb-Nup54/58 interaction. Yb interacts with Nup54/58 only when they are assembled into the NPC, as C-terminal deletions that prevent Nup-Nup interactions reduced Yb binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by co-IP experiments with domain deletion mutants. The partial requirement for the HelC domain (C116-C117) and dependence on NPC assembly (C118) are clearly demonstrated. The data appropriately acknowledge that the HelC domain is not solely responsible for the interaction.

results.result: Nxf1, but not Nup54/58, directly binds flam RNA. CLIP-seq with HALO-tagged proteins showed that Nup54 and Nup58 failed to enrich for flam RNA, while Nxf1 showed interaction toward the 5' end of the flam transcript, which undergoes splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by CLIP-seq data with appropriate controls. The negative result for Nup54/58 (C99) and positive result for Nxf1 (C100) are clearly stated. The 5' enrichment for Nxf1 is consistent with co-transcriptional loading following splicing.

results.result: Yb localizes proximally to the cytoplasmic filaments of the NPC but is not an integral NPC component. Yb PL-MS enriched for known interactors (Armi, Piwi) but only one Nup (Nup214, which localizes to cytoplasmic filaments), indicating Yb is not stably integrated into the NPC structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by PL-MS data with appropriate positive controls (known Yb interactors). The detection of only cytoplasmic Nup214 (C102) and absence of other Nups supports the inference that Yb is not an integral NPC component (C103) but associates with the cytoplasmic side.

results.result: Physical associations between Yb and Nup54/58 are likely transient, and Nup54/58 are not confined to discrete sites on the nuclear envelope. Immunofluorescence showed Yb-bodies were often distinct from Nup foci, with Nup signal distributed along the entire nuclear envelope. This suggests flam export might only be initiated where Nup54/58 contact Yb, nucleating Yb-body assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing spatial relationships between Yb and Nups. The inference about transient interactions (C108) is reasonable given the PL-MS and imaging data. The hypothesis about export initiation (C110) is appropriately speculative and consistent with the data.

results.result: Yb-body formation depends on flam RNA and is interdependent with flam transcript production and localization. Trans-heterozygous flamBG/KG mutants showed disassembly of Yb-bodies despite residual Yb protein, and knockdowns of nxf1/nxt1 compromised Yb-body formation, suggesting interdependence between flam production, export, and Yb-body assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C40, C42-C43 are supported by genetic and knockdown experiments with imaging data. The observation that Yb protein persists without Yb-bodies in flam mutants (C40) and that export factor depletion affects Yb-bodies (C42) supports the interdependence model (C43).

results.result: Proposed model: Nup54/58 ensure processivity of flam export, with residual exported transcripts processed by Yb at lower efficiency. The Nxf1-NPC-Yb axis coordinates initiation, processivity, and directionality of flam export through export-coupled licensing. Disruption leads to nuclear confinement and destabilization of flam transcripts, possibly with feedback to transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C121, C124-C126, C129 represent a proposed mechanistic model that integrates the experimental findings. While the model is consistent with the data, several aspects remain speculative (appropriately acknowledged in the text). Key mechanistic details about processivity, transcript handoff between factors, and transcriptional feedback require additional experimental validation.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Nup54 and Nup58 are specifically required for TE regulation in follicle cells by enabling flam export and piRNA production, distinct from general NPC function. They interact with both nuclear (Nxf1/Nxt1) and cytoplasmic (Yb) components, bridging nuclear export to cytosolic fate specification, and function from within the NPC.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123, C127-C128, C130-C131 summarize the major findings that are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript. The specificity (C123), bridging function (C127-C128), and NPC localization (C130) are all supported by multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Broader implications: Some Nups can acquire specialized tissue-specific roles, and genomic loci under strong selective pressure can exploit NPC subunits to facilitate expression. This represents a potential paradigm for co-option of FG-Nups for specific transcript trafficking routes in a cell-type-specific manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C17, C134-C136 represent broader interpretations and implications of the findings. The tissue-specificity (C6) is well-demonstrated by the data. The evolutionary implications (C8, C136) are reasonable extrapolations but appropriately speculative. The comparison with Nup358 (C134) provides additional support for tissue-specific Nup functions.

results.result: Speculation on nucleoporopathies: Tissue-specific control of export routes might explain nucleoporopathies, where Nup mutations cause tissue-specific phenotypes despite ubiquitous expression. Tissue-specific phenotypes might stem from specialized roles in regulating genes essential for that tissue's function.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 represent speculative connections to human disease. While C137 cites established knowledge about Nup evolution, the hypotheses about nucleoporopathies (C138-C139) are extrapolations from the Drosophila findings without direct experimental support. These remain interesting hypotheses requiring future investigation.

results.result: Background knowledge: Established facts about NPC structure and function, piRNA pathway biology, flamenco locus characteristics, Yb-body properties, and relevant prior genetic findings. These claims provide context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C16, C18-C45, C62-C64, C98, C115, C120, C132 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide necessary background and context for interpreting the new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are standard in the field.

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 have specialized roles in transposon silencing in Drosophila ovarian follicle cells, specifically affecting flamenco-derived piRNA biogenesis without severely impacting cell viability or general gene expression, unlike other Nup depletions.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers acknowledge this as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states the work is 'informative and conservatively interpreted' regarding OSC experiments. Reviewer 2 notes 'the observations support that Nup54 and Nup58 have a dedicated role in flam RNA export' and that the experiments are 'well-controlled' with 'extremely convincing' results. Reviewer 3 confirms 'it is thoroughly convincing that there is a unique requirement for Nup54 and Nup58 in piRNA biogenesis, specifically from the flam locus.'

results.result: Loss of Nup54/58 leads to reduced flam transcript levels with a 3' bias, suggesting these nucleoporins ensure processivity of nuclear export of the long flam transcript, which becomes destabilized when export is compromised.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises a critical alternative interpretation: 'Given the bias towards loss of 3′ transcript coverage and piRNA abundance, together with both the involvement of the TREX complex in piRNA biogenesis and the role of nuclear pore proteins in transcriptional elongation, isn't it more likely that Nup54/58 promote transcriptional elongation across the entirety of flam or that they prevent premature termination in the 3′ region?' Reviewer 2 accepts the data showing 'Instability increases towards the 3'end of the flam locus' but the mechanistic interpretation remains contested.

results.result: Knockdown of nup54 and nup58 results in a specific ~3-fold decrease in flam-derived piRNAs with a 3' bias, while piRNAs from other sources remain unaffected, contrasting with the general piRNA loss observed in yb knockdowns.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'siNup54/58 specifically affect the stability of flam piRNAs while siYb affects the levels of different types of piRNAs indicating a specific role for Nup54/58 in flam piRNA biogenesis/maturation that is distinct from Yb.' The specificity of the effect is noted as convincing by multiple reviewers.

results.result: Depletion of Nup54/58 causes flam RNA to accumulate in a nuclear focus at the nuclear envelope, likely representing stalled export, while bulk mRNA export remains unaffected.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'Loss of Nup54/58 affects flam RNA detection in the cytoplasm, but not in the nucleus where it is detected as a dot corresponding to the flam locus associated with the nuclear periphery' and that 'RNAseq/Proseq and imaging data support the view that Nup54/58 may ensure processivity of flam nuclear export.' The specificity for flam versus bulk mRNA is accepted as demonstrated.

results.result: The C-terminal domains of Nup54 and Nup58, required for their interaction and NPC assembly, are critical for TE silencing function, while the FG-repeat regions are dispensable, suggesting these nucleoporins function from within the NPC.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises significant concerns: 'A key concern is that it is well established that nups can function outside of the NPC, both at genomic loci and also in the cytoplasm but this is not fully considered or ruled out' and 'how these domains could connect to Nxf1 without FG-repeats remains difficult to rationalize.' While the data on domain requirements are accepted, the interpretation that function occurs 'from within the NPC' is questioned.

results.result: The nup54MB mutant allele, producing a truncated protein lacking the C-terminal domain, shows TE de-repression, reduced flam RNA levels, and decreased Yb-bodies in vivo, confirming the in vitro findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern about interpretation: 'since the mutant ovaries are small...the cell composition of the controls and mutants will be quite different' and requests 'A detailed description of the experimental evidence that explains why the authors' normalization strategy allows such a comparison' and to 'show (e.g., by in situ hybridization) that TE expression is in fact higher in vivo in identical cell types.' The data are presented but normalization and cell-type specificity concerns remain unaddressed.

results.result: Nup54 and Nup58 physically interact with both Yb and Nxf1/Nxt1, with Yb enriched in Nup54/58 proximity-labeling mass spectrometry and the interaction being RNA-independent, suggesting these nucleoporins bridge nuclear export to cytosolic fate specification.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes a critical inconsistency: 'Yb does not efficiently interact with Nup54/58 nor Nxf1 by mass spec. It is unexpected that Yb does not interact with Nxf1, since Nxf1 is expected to transport flam RNAs to the cytoplasmic side of the NPC through interactions with Nup54/Nup58 in order to deliver the transcripts to Yb' and asks 'When does Yb bind Flam transcripts and wouldn't it be expected that Yb interacts with Nxf1/Nxt1 to take over the flam transcripts?' The asymmetry in detection between different methods raises questions about the model.

results.result: Yb proximity-labeling detected only Nup214 among nucleoporins, suggesting Yb localizes near cytoplasmic NPC filaments but is not stably anchored, with transient associations with Nup54/58 at specific pores potentially nucleating Yb-body assembly.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questions the spatial relationship: 'this figure indicates that the Yb bodies and the flam DNA don't show an obvious proximity or correlation (on either side of the NPC). This is unexpected based on the model that Nup54/58 establish a physical connection between Nxf1/Nxt1-bound flam RNAs and their delivery to Yb bodies on the cytoplasmic side of the NPC.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Invoking a model that suggests that Yb might act similarly to Dbp5 on the cytosolic filaments is certainly interesting, but the data do not yet support this.'

results.result: The authors propose a model where the Nxf1-NPC-Yb axis coordinates initiation, processivity, and directionality of flam export, with Nup54/58 functioning from within the pore to bridge nuclear and cytoplasmic components.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the data are on the whole supportive of the proposed model' but notes unresolved questions. Reviewer 3 is more critical: 'the proposed model is not fully supported by the data' and 'The suggestion is to be more circumspect with the proposed model and to consider alternative possibilities.' Reviewer 1 requests discussion of 'alternative explanations more consonant with the nucleopore literature.'

results.result: Yb-body formation depends on flam RNA and is disrupted by loss of Nup54/58 or Nxf1/Nxt1, indicating interdependence between flam transcript production, localization, and Yb-body assembly.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'By fluorescence imaging approaches, they also show that Yb formation in OSCs depends on correct flam expression and functional Nxf1/Nxt1 export factors' and that these observations are well-supported. The interdependence is accepted as demonstrated, though mechanistic details remain to be elucidated.

results.result: Knockdown of most other Nups, including Nup62 and Nup93-1, causes widespread effects on gene expression, cell viability, and non-specific TE de-repression, contrasting with the specific effects of Nup54/58 depletion.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'Knock down of Nup62 and Nup93 results in flam expression defects and upregulation of transposons as well as deregulation of multiple genes. In contrast, knock down of Yb, Nup54 and Nup58 leads to loss or dispersed Yb-bodies, decreased flam RNA levels as well as increased TE expression without substantially affecting overall gene expression or viability.' This contrast is accepted as demonstrated.

results.result: CLIP-seq experiments showed that Nxf1 interacts with the 5' end of flam transcripts, while Nup54 and Nup58 CLIP-seq failed to enrich for flam RNA.
results.evaluation: This negative result for Nup54/58 and positive result for Nxf1 is presented as data without reviewer challenge, though it contributes to the uncertainty about direct RNA binding by the nucleoporins.

results.result: PRO-seq data show that Nup54/58 or Yb knockdown has minimal effect on transcription initiation or early elongation at flam, though siYb shows decreased signal across the entire locus, possibly indicating feedback from disrupted export to transcription.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 asks 'How could loss of Yb affect flam transcription efficiency?' acknowledging the observation while seeking clarification. The data are accepted but the feedback mechanism remains speculative.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the specialized role of Nup54/58 in transposon control (C3, C4, C47-C61, C122-C123). OpenEval finds the claims SUPPORTED with converging evidence from RNA-seq, viability assays, and imaging. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED, with all three reviewers acknowledging it as a key finding with 'extremely convincing' and 'thoroughly convincing' results. Strong agreement on this core finding.

Both address the 3' bias in flam transcript reduction (C65-C71, C81-C82). OpenEval finds the post-transcriptional instability interpretation SUPPORTED by RNA-seq and PRO-seq data. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 proposing an alternative interpretation involving transcriptional elongation defects rather than export/stability issues. Significant disagreement on mechanistic interpretation despite accepting the data.

Both evaluate flam-specific piRNA loss with 3' bias (C73-C77). Perfect claim overlap (Jaccard=1.0). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by small RNA-seq with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 explicitly noting the specificity is convincing. Strong agreement on both data quality and interpretation.

Both evaluate RNA-FISH data showing flam nuclear retention (C78-C80). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 noting the data support the view that Nup54/58 ensure processivity of flam nuclear export. Agreement on the specificity for flam versus bulk mRNA.

Both evaluate domain deletion experiments (C84-C87, C96-C97). Perfect claim overlap (Jaccard=1.0). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED and concludes function occurs within the NPC. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 raising concerns that nups can function outside the NPC and questioning how domains connect to Nxf1 without FG-repeats. Agreement on data, disagreement on localization interpretation.

Both evaluate in vivo validation with nup54 mutant allele (C88-C95). Perfect claim overlap (Jaccard=1.0). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN due to concerns about normalization strategy and cell composition differences between mutant and control ovaries. Reviewer 1 requests additional evidence for cell-type-specific TE expression. Disagreement on adequacy of experimental controls.

Both evaluate CLIP-seq results (C99-C100). Perfect claim overlap (Jaccard=1.0). OpenEval finds the negative result for Nup54/58 and positive result for Nxf1 SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED without challenge, though it contributes to uncertainty about direct RNA binding by nucleoporins. Agreement on the data.

Both evaluate interdependence of Yb-bodies and flam (C36, C40, C42-C43). High claim overlap (Jaccard=0.8). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by genetic and imaging data. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 noting the observations are well-supported, though mechanistic details remain to be elucidated. Agreement on demonstrated interdependence.

Both evaluate protein interaction data (C104-C107, C112-C114, C116-C118). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by PL-MS and co-IP data showing RNA-independent Nup54/58-Yb interaction. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 noting a critical inconsistency: Yb does not efficiently interact with Nup54/58 or Nxf1 by mass spec, which is unexpected given the proposed model. Disagreement on interpretation of interaction data asymmetry.

Both evaluate spatial relationships and transient interactions (C102-C103, C108-C110). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by immunofluorescence and PL-MS data. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 noting Yb bodies and flam DNA don't show obvious proximity, which is unexpected based on the model. Reviewer 3 notes the Dbp5 analogy is interesting but not yet supported. Disagreement on spatial model support.

Both address domain requirements for Yb interaction (C116-C118). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by co-IP with domain deletion mutants. Peer reviewers group this with broader interaction data marked UNCERTAIN due to inconsistencies in mass spec versus co-IP results. Partial overlap in claims evaluated.

Both evaluate Yb's relationship to NPC (C102-C103). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED that Yb is not an integral NPC component but associates with cytoplasmic side. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN due to spatial relationship concerns and lack of obvious proximity between Yb bodies and flam DNA. Disagreement on model support.

Both evaluate the overall mechanistic model (C82-C83, C121, C124-C126, C129-C130). OpenEval marks this UNCERTAIN, acknowledging speculative aspects requiring validation. Peer reviewers also mark this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 stating 'the proposed model is not fully supported by the data' and requesting more circumspect presentation with alternative possibilities. Agreement that model remains speculative.

Both address major findings summary (C122-C123). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as well-demonstrated by experimental data. Peer reviewers also find the core specificity finding SUPPORTED. Agreement on the main conclusions about Nup54/58 specialized role.

Both address bridging function and NPC localization (C127-C128, C130-C131). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by multiple lines of evidence. Peer reviewers mark related claims UNCERTAIN due to concerns about whether function truly occurs within NPC versus at other locations. Disagreement on localization certainty.

Both evaluate specificity of Nup54/58 effects versus other Nups (C46, C58-C60). OpenEval finds the comparison strengthens the specificity claim. Peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED, accepting the contrast between Nup54/58 and Nup62/Nup93 knockdowns. Agreement on demonstrated specificity.

Both address PRO-seq controls and transcriptional feedback (C69-C70, C126). OpenEval finds PRO-seq controls strengthen post-transcriptional interpretation. Peer reviewers accept the observation but note the feedback mechanism remains speculative. Partial agreement on data, uncertainty about mechanism.

OpenEval evaluates broader implications including tissue-specificity (C6-C8, C17, C134-C136). Finds tissue-specificity well-demonstrated but evolutionary implications appropriately speculative. No corresponding focused peer review evaluation found, though these contextual claims are not challenged.

OpenEval evaluates speculative connections to human disease and nucleoporopathies (C137-C139). Marks these UNCERTAIN as extrapolations requiring future investigation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these speculative disease connections.

OpenEval evaluates established background knowledge from literature (C1-C2, C9-C45, C62-C64, C98, C115, C120, C132). Finds these appropriately cited and standard in the field. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate background/citation claims.
